tldr: RoCo is a zero-shot multi-robot collaboration method that uses LLMs for both high-level dialogue-based task coordination and low-level motion planning, validated on a new 6-task benchmark called RoCoBench.
contributions: An LLM-based multi-robot framework (RoCo) enabling dialogue-style task coordination, feedback-improved sub-task planning, and LLM-informed multi-arm motion planning in joint space
RoCoBench, a 6-task benchmark covering diverse collaboration scenarios varying in task decomposition, observation space symmetry, and workspace overlap
RoCoBench-Text, a text-only dataset for evaluating LLM agent representation and reasoning in multi-agent collaboration
methods: Each robot is delegated an LLM agent that engages in a dialogue to reason about task strategy, producing a sub-task plan. The plan is validated through text parsing, task constraint checking, inverse kinematics feasibility, collision checking, and waypoint validation, with environment feedback looped back to agents for re-planning. Validated plans are converted into goal configurations in joint space and executed via a centralized RRT-based multi-arm motion planner. LLMs also generate 3D task-space waypoints to reduce motion planner sample complexity.
results: RoCo achieves high success rates across all 6 tasks in RoCoBench. In a 3D spatial reasoning toy example with GPT-4, 86.7% success rate over 30 runs with an average of 2.73 attempts. Dialogue agents sometimes achieve comparable performance to an oracle planner despite receiving less information. LLM-proposed waypoints significantly accelerate motion planning for placing sub-tasks under high workspace overlap. Real-world experiments with a robot and human sorting blocks show performance bottlenecked by OWL-ViT object detection accuracy. Zero-shot adaptation demonstrated across object initialization, task goal, and robot capability variations.
limitations: LLM 3D spatial reasoning degrades as grid size and number of obstacles increase
Plans may fail IK checks or collision checks, requiring re-planning rounds
Episode is considered failed if task is not completed within a finite number of rounds
Real-world performance bottlenecked by imperfect perception from object detection models (e.g., OWL-ViT errors)
Maximum re-plan attempts per round limits recovery from persistent failures
